title: COC: the metric that prices cancellations in the currency of customer acquisition
summary: Jason Cohen introduces COC (Cost of Cancellations) = payback period × monthly revenue churn, the share of revenue a SaaS company must spend each month just to avoid shrinking. It shows churn alone is a third of the story and that CAC, ARPC and net negative churn matter just as much.

principles.text: Measure the cost of churn as COC = payback period (p) × monthly revenue cancellation rate (c): the share of revenue spent just to stay level.
principles.quote:
**The *percentage* of our revenue we'll have to spend this month, just to keep from shrinking**:

`COC = p ✕ c`

principles.text: Payback period equals CAC divided by ARPC, which is also the cost to acquire one more dollar of MRR.
principles.quote: `p` = "the cost to acquire one more dollar of MRR" = `CAC / ARPC`

principles.text: Cancellations eat a startling share of revenue: a healthy SMB SaaS (3% churn, 7-month payback) spends 21% of revenue a month just to stay flat.
principles.quote: In this case, `COC = 0.21`, which means a whopping 21% of its revenue *every month* will be spent *just keeping revenues level.*

principles.text: A short payback period can overwhelm a bad cancellation rate; a long payback with the same churn is deadly.
principles.quote: a very good pay-back period can overwhelm a crappy cancellation rate.

principles.text: Metrics literature fixates on churn, but COC shows there are three levers: cancellations, CAC and ARPC. When churn has a floor, shift CAC or ARPC instead.
principles.quote: **typical metrics literature focuses only on reducing cancellation rate, which is only a third of the story.**

principles.text: Treat c as net churn (cancellations plus downgrades minus upgrades). Reaching zero net churn makes COC zero, so build upsell paths.
principles.quote: **getting to zero net churn is the strongest thing you can do** in terms of COC.
